title: 4 Physician Scheduling Options for Private Practices
description: Physician scheduling for private practices and provider groups: managed services, spreadsheets, self-service software and EHR-native modules.
content:
Summary

  • Physicians on r/hospitalist describe spending 4-8 hours a month just on the first draft of a schedule, before swaps and changes.
  • There are four categories of scheduling tools, covering five named tools and services, each designed to solve a different problem, from patient booking to internal provider coordination.
  • Most tools focus on what happens after a schedule is made (viewing or filling it), not the complex task of creating a fair physician schedule from scratch.
  • If your core problem is the time and complexity of building fair call, rotation, and clinic schedules, a managed service like Scheduling Wizard is designed to solve it for you.

You built your practice around medicine, not spreadsheets. Yet somehow, a surprising chunk of your week gets swallowed by the scheduling puzzle: who's on call Thursday, who swapped last weekend, whether the fairness math still holds up across the quarter. According to physicians on forums like r/hospitalist, it takes anywhere from 4 to 8 hours a month just to produce the first draft of a schedule, and that's before the swaps, last-minute changes, and "can you just carry it in your head" fairness tracking that adds up all month long.

There are plenty of tools. The catch is that they solve different problems, and picking from the wrong category means paying for something that does not touch the part that takes your time.

This guide breaks down five private practice physician scheduling tools and services across four categories. For each, we cover what it is built for and where it stops, so you can match the category to the problem you actually have.

1. Managed Scheduling Services

Best for: Complex multi-provider practices that want to stop building schedules entirely.

This is the category practices hear about least. A managed scheduling service is a team, not software: you send your rules, coverage requirements, physician preferences and fairness rules, and you get back a finished schedule. There is nothing to learn or configure, and nobody has to carry the logic in their head.

Scheduling Wizard

Scheduling Wizard is our entry in this category. A YC-backed (W26) managed service, Scheduling Wizard is a team that builds schedules full time: complete Block, Clinic, Call, and Attending schedules. You submit your rules (vacation requests, elective preferences, coverage minimums, fairness rules) and receive the finished schedule, delivered as Excel or Google Sheets, or on a custom live view we build for you. Whether it goes into the platform your practice already uses, the live view, or both is entirely up to you.

The build is only part of the work. As one hospitalist put it, "swapping duties last minute and maintaining fairness over months... that's what really adds up." Scheduling Wizard takes the build and the fairness arithmetic off your team.

How it differs from enterprise software: platforms like QGenda give a practice capable tools, but someone has to learn and run them. As one physician wrote on Reddit, "getting QG to actually do what you want isn't easy, and learning how it works is very complicated." With Scheduling Wizard there is no software to master, and your rules stay written down with us when your senior scheduler leaves. We hold the fairness and coverage targets in the build, rather than leaving you to track them by hand.

Key capabilities include:

  • Call schedules with fair call distribution
  • Block/rotation and clinic schedule coordination
  • Physician preference integration (vacation, conferences, clinic days)
  • Coverage built to your minimums at every site
  • Redrafts around unplanned absences

Ideal use case: Private practices with 10+ providers, complex call structures or several sites, where building the schedule by hand has become a real cost.

Key limitations: Less suited for practices that want to make constant real-time manual micro-adjustments themselves. This is a service model, not a self-serve dashboard.

Cost: quoted per group, and best weighed against what physician or administrator time on scheduling costs you now.

2. Excel / Google Sheets

Best for: Practices whose coverage rules and partner arrangements change faster than any platform can be reconfigured.

Many practice schedules are still built in a spreadsheet, which is why it belongs second rather than last. It will take contract terms, site splits, partner preferences and the arrangements that were never written down, and it will take them the moment you think of them. Google Sheets lets the whole group work in one file and see what changed.

What it does not do is the counting. Call equity across a year, weekend and holiday balance, and coverage minimums at every site are arithmetic, and arithmetic done by hand between clinics is where disputes start. It also holds the schedule without holding the reasoning, so it does not transfer when the person who built it steps back.

3. Self-Service Scheduling Software

Best for: Solo practitioners and small single-specialty practices with straightforward booking needs.

Self-service scheduling software is the most accessible category: SaaS tools you buy, configure, and manage yourself. They're designed to help practices set up online appointment booking, automated reminders, and patient intake forms without requiring a large IT team.

Acuity Scheduling

Acuity Scheduling is a well-known tool in this tier. It allows practices to offer 24/7 online booking, send automated appointment reminders to reduce no-shows, and collect intake information before the visit. It's intuitive to set up and works well for straightforward, appointment-based scheduling flows.

Key limitations: Acuity is built for patient appointment booking. It suits a solo dermatologist booking cosmetic consults; it is not designed for a hospitalist group managing call shifts, swaps and fairness across 20 physicians.

Healthie

Healthie is another self-service option popular among smaller practices, particularly in the behavioral health and wellness space. It includes scheduling alongside telehealth, billing, and charting in a lightweight package. Still, like most self-service tools, it's built around patient appointment booking, not the harder job of building a provider schedule.

Ideal use case: A solo or small-group practice with simple, repeatable appointment types and no complex call or rotation scheduling requirements.

Key limitations: These tools are built for appointment flows rather than provider schedules. If your scheduling involves variable shift lengths (8h, 24h, full weeks), fairness balancing or several sites, you will need something else for that part.

4. EHR-Native Schedulers

Best for: Mid-to-large practices or hospital-affiliated groups already deeply embedded in an EHR ecosystem.

EHR-native scheduling modules are built directly into systems like Epic, Cerner, or Meditech, or designed as deeply integrated companions to them. The core value proposition is a single source of truth: patient data, appointments, clinical notes, and billing all live in one system, reducing the risk of data silos and manual data re-entry.

Luma Health

Luma Health is a well-known example. It integrates with EHR systems and automates patient outreach, reminders and scheduling inside the practice's existing clinical workflow. If your team already lives inside an EHR all day, Luma Health extends that environment rather than adding another platform to manage.

Key limitations: These modules are built around patient appointment flow. Balancing a provider call schedule, tracking swaps and rotation rules is a different job, and changes to the module usually go through the vendor or internal IT.

Ideal use case: Practices where data integration and a unified patient record are the primary concern, and where provider schedule complexity is relatively low.

Cost: usually tied to your EHR contract.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the main difference between Scheduling Wizard and software like QGenda or Amion?

Scheduling Wizard is a service that builds your physician schedule for you, while QGenda and Amion are platforms your team runs to build, publish and manage the schedule. We build the finished schedule and deliver it as Excel or Google Sheets, or on a custom live view we build for you. What happens next is entirely up to you: upload it into your existing platform, use our live view, or both. We take on the hours spent building the schedule.

What rules does a managed service build a practice schedule around?

Coverage minimums first, then call equity, contractual obligations, time off and requests, and multiple sites where the practice has them. During onboarding we collect all of it, including the rules nobody writes down, and build the schedule around them. A practice has no ACGME requirement; that applies to residency and fellowship programs, and we build those too.

What if our group is attached to a training program?

Then two sets of rules apply at once, and they interact. The residents and fellows carry the ACGME duty hour requirements, including at-home call activity counting toward the 80-hour limit (averaged over four weeks). The attendings carry the group's own coverage and supervision obligations. We build both schedules together so one does not break the other.

What happens when something changes mid-year, like a leave or a new site?

You tell us what changed and we rebuild the rest of the schedule to the same rules, with coverage and fairness intact. Redrafts through the year are part of the service.

Who is the ideal user for a managed scheduling service?

The ideal user is any medical group, private practice, or residency program that finds the process of building, balancing, and maintaining physician schedules to be a significant administrative burden. This service is best for groups with 10+ providers, complex call or rotation structures, multi-site coverage needs, or a training program attached to the group. If you're spending more than a few hours each month on scheduling spreadsheets, the model is likely to fit.

Why is Scheduling Wizard a service rather than self-serve software?

Scheduling Wizard is a service because building a fair physician schedule to every rule at once is specialized work, not a simple configuration task. With self-serve software, someone in your group still has to learn the tool and keep the scheduling logic current. By providing a "done-for-you" service, we remove the burden of learning new software and take the build off your plate, with fairness and coverage as part of it.

How are physician preferences and vacation requests handled?

All physician preferences, including vacation requests, conference dates, and specific call/shift preferences, are submitted as inputs before the schedule is built. Our team builds around them as far as the coverage rules allow, and tells you where a request could not be honored and why, so the trade-off is yours rather than a surprise.
